7.1: The story press worked, and the garden remained open. On the familiar path, Nib stopped to listen. The brook sounded unusually quiet, and less water showed between its usual stones. Lark brought the field notebook, the ordinary viewing lens, and a borrowed channel diagram. The moonstone stayed at camp; this question needed observations.

“A useful observation note gives a place, a time, and what we actually notice,” Lark explained gently. “I can supply the word quiet; it isn't an independent spelling task today. Read note and brook, then keep what we see separate from our ideas about why.”
“Which picture records the change beside this same path?” Lark invited gently. “What can we record before choosing an explanation?”

Lark dated the notebook's new observation. Nib drew the same stones with the lower visible water, leaving space below for questions. A brook taking a nap was an amusing idea, not a measured cause. The diagram offered a way to inspect the upstream route without deciding the answer in advance.
The brook is low. I can see the bank.
“What does the passage report about the brook?” Lark asked gently. “Does it tell us why?”
Your first investigation page kept the question open. The crew packed the notebook and followed the dry path toward the fixed bridge, ready to use the diagram's arrows.
7.2: Nib turned the channel diagram until its prettiest tree matched a nearby trunk. The bridge in the drawing then pointed in an impossible direction. Lark set the page against the real fixed bridge instead. Inlet, gate, alternate route, and outlet could now keep the same relationship on paper and ground.

“A diagram's arrows tell us relationships and direction,” Lark explained clearly. “Read in-let and out-let as joined familiar parts. We'll orient the page to the fixed bridge before following an arrow, then check that its endpoint matches the place we reach.”
“Read inlet and outlet on the chart,” Lark invited gently. “Which arrow gives the first upstream inspection?”

Nib walked along the dry route beside the inlet arrow. Lark checked its endpoint against the real access place. They reached the intended inspection point without entering the water or turning a control. A keeper's crowded page waited in the notebook pocket, describing what had last been noticed here.
The inlet is at the top. The outlet is at the end.
“Which label belongs at the end in this little diagram description?” Lark asked gently. “Use the second sentence.”
Your journal kept the oriented chart. The bridge stayed the fixed reference. Now the crew had to find the useful water observations among the keeper page's many other details.
7.3: The keeper's page mentioned weather, a picnic, and observations from two water points. Nib chose the picnic as the most promising detail. Lark enjoyed its sandwich drawing, then placed the quiet-brook question beside the page. The most interesting sentence was not necessarily the one that helped answer it.

“A main idea must fit the useful details,” Lark explained gently. “First ask what question we are trying to answer. Then read for the sentences that bear on it. We can enjoy the picnic without treating it as evidence about the water route.”
“Read the short page, then find its two water observations,” Lark invited gently. “Which detail belongs to another topic?”

The page placed water at one recorded point and none at the other. Lark underlined those sentences after the reading. They narrowed the question to the route between the points. Neither sentence yet showed what had changed that route. Nib left the picnic drawing in its margin, interesting and properly separate.
The inlet is wet. The outlet is dry. A cake is on the mat.
“Which two sentences help with the water question?” Lark asked gently. “Which one tells us something else?”
Your journal gained a smaller question, supported by the right details. The crew would need an observation that could distinguish a dry supply from water taking a different path.
7.4: Lark wondered whether the supply had dried. Nib wondered whether the gate sent water somewhere else. Both ideas could explain a quieter brook from a distance. Neither was proved by sounding sensible. The channel diagram showed where their predictions would differ.

“An if statement makes a prediction we can check,” Lark explained clearly. “If no water reaches the inlet, a direct inlet look should show that. If water is arriving but taking another route, the observation should differ. Our preferred story must wait for the check.”
“Which observation would help separate the two ideas?” Lark invited gently. “Use the diagram to choose a place where their predictions differ.”

The crew planned a direct inlet and gate inspection from the fixed dry platform. Lark wrote the predictions on separate lines. Nib packed the notebook instead of a repair tool. Before changing anything, they would read how to approach and record the scene without destroying the evidence they came to inspect.
If the inlet is dry, the brook can be dry. If the inlet is wet, look at the gate.
“What check follows a wet inlet in this plan?” Lark asked gently. “Is an if sentence a result we already observed?”
Your journal now held possibilities and a useful next check. The route was chosen for information, not because either friend's first explanation had won a vote.
7.5: At the approach, Nib reached toward a handle. Lark opened the how-to page. Its first picture showed a person looking from the dry platform with a notebook. The handle belonged to a later step. Moving it now would change the very arrangement they wanted to understand.

“Read the instructions in order, keeping their goal in view,” Lark explained gently. “Look and record come before change. First and then help us connect the steps. We can leave the page open beside its matching pictures rather than remember every word at once.”
“Read the first two directions,” Lark invited gently. “Which action belongs before touching a control?”

Nib put his paw back beside the notebook. They followed the dry approach and stopped at the fixed viewing position. The gate was visible, but a loose old label made the alternate channel hard to identify. They recorded that uncertainty instead of moving the gate to see what happened.
First look at the gate. Then make a note.
“What comes before making the note?” Lark asked gently. “Does either sentence ask us to move the gate?”
Your journal kept the untouched scene. The next job was matching labels to their real anchors, so the crew could describe the channels accurately before testing an explanation.
7.6: A loose label lay beside the wrong channel. Nib trusted its landing place until Lark noticed its old mounting holes. On the diagram, the label's anchor belonged to a supported post beside the alternate route. The water control had not moved just because its sign had fallen.

“A label needs its correct connection,” Lark explained clearly. “Read the word, follow its diagram anchor, and compare the actual mounting holes. Moving a loose sign back to its post can repair our description without changing the water arrangement we are investigating.”
“Match the alternate-channel label to its original post,” Lark invited gently. “Which anchor agrees with both the chart and the real holes?”

Nib replaced the loose label on its original support. Lark checked inlet, gate, alternate channel, and usual brook against the same diagram. They could now describe the scene without trusting where a fallen sign happened to lie. The keeper's older dry-weather note could be compared with today's observation fairly.
The pool is past the gate. The gap is by the bank.
“What lies past the gate in the short description?” Lark asked gently. “Where does it put the gap?”
Your journal gained corrected labels while the control stayed untouched. Next came two records from different mornings, each with its own time and place.
7.7: The older note described a genuinely dry period. Today's note recorded water at the inlet. Lark's first explanation had fitted the older page, and she had nearly carried it into the present without checking its date. Nib placed both notes beside the current diagram.

“Two records can both be accurate about different moments,” Lark explained thoughtfully. “Read each source's place and time before deciding that they disagree. Then compare the current observation with the prediction we wrote for a dry supply.”
“Which note describes today's inlet?” Lark invited gently. “What does it make us reconsider about the dry-supply idea?”

Lark marked her earlier explanation as a possibility no longer fitting the current inlet observation. She did not erase the old note or pretend it had been false. Nib kept today's water observation beside the revised question. With the keeper, they could now inspect the branch and gate directly from the prepared position.
At first, the inlet had no flow. At this check, the inlet is wet.
“Do the sentences describe the same check?” Lark asked gently. “Which words show a change of time?”

Your journal preserved the changed explanation and the evidence that changed it. Lark closed the older note carefully. The next observation would show the actual branch-gate relationship rather than merely predict one.
7.8: From the fixed platform, the keeper showed the trapped branch. It held the old gate in the alternate-routing position. The crew could finally see that physical relationship directly. Lark recorded the before state. Nib traced the usual brook and alternate channel on the unchanged diagram.

“Keep action and result on different lines,” Lark explained clearly. “The process page tells the keeper what to do. Our next observation tells us what happened afterward. A repair that sounds sensible still needs its result checked.”
“Read and order the visible process steps,” Lark invited gently. “What happens to the branch before the supported gate is reset?”

The keeper removed the trapped branch and reset the gate on its supports. Nib stayed on the dry platform with the notebook. Water followed the usual channel again. Lark recorded that observed result separately from the repair action. They planned a later check rather than treating one moment of returning flow as every answer they might need.
First lift the branch. Then set the gate.
“Which action comes first?” Lark asked gently. “Does this process passage itself tell us the later result?”

Your journal now held before, action, and result. The branch-gate cause had been directly checked. A visitor could use that explanation, while questions the notes had never measured still remained open.
7.9: A visitor asked what changed and whether every animal had returned. Nib opened the notebook confidently, then stopped. It held a repair record, but no animal count. Lark set the two questions beside the page so each could be judged against the information actually there.

“A useful page can answer some questions and leave others open,” Lark explained gently. “Find the sentence supporting an answer. If no observation or count was recorded, say that the page does not tell us. We can choose a new limited observation without inventing an old one.”
“Which question can our repair page answer?” Lark invited gently. “Which one would need a different observation?”

The notes supported the branch-and-gate explanation and the observed return of flow. They did not support a claim about every animal. Nib left that answer open. The crew planned a limited follow-up at the same brook view. A new morning note was kept closed until its first reading in the final chapter.
The branch held the gate. The page has no count.
“What does the page lack?” Lark asked gently. “Which question could that missing information affect?”

Your journal became more useful because it kept its limits visible. The repair was complete. The final visit would compare a fresh note with the same familiar brook rather than pretend to count every living thing.
7.10: The new morning note lay face down beside the notebook. Nib kept its answer to himself. Lark brought the crew to the same dry viewing place used at the beginning, leaving the fresh words covered until you were ready. The older observations and repair record stayed available for comparison.

“This is a fresh page with familiar spellings,” Lark explained warmly. “Try its words before I read them aloud. You can ask for help with any part. Then we'll compare what it says with the same place we recorded before.”
“Read the new note,” Lark invited gently. “What does it report, and what can we check by looking from here?”

After the reading, the crew compared the note with the actual gate and usual brook. Lark added the limited follow-up observation beside the before-and-after record. The ordinary field lens joined your collection. Observations, predictions, actions, and results remained distinct as the journal pages became a finished book.
The gate is up. The brook is in the sun.
“Where does the note put the brook?” Lark asked gently. “Does it tell us how many animals are here?”

Field Notes joined the library as the seventh finished adventure. The brook mystery had a local cause, an ordinary repair, and a checked result. Beside the old atlas waited a blank route page for a later expedition the child could choose and lead.
